note: CDFW's Shark Incident Database, shaped for the app with species and activity AS RECORDED, plus CDFW's own framing quotes (incident definition, the incident-not-attack preference, rarity, nursery grounds) verified against a snapshot of the White Shark page. Coverage ends at the snapshot's own last date — the app must display that and link to CDFW for anything newer, never implying currency through today.

quotes.incident_definition: The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) defines a shark incident as any documented case where a shark approached and touched a person in the water, or touched a person’s surfboard, kayak, paddleboard, etc. This does not include shark sightings where no contact occurred, instances where sharks approached boats, or cases where hooked sharks caused injury or damage.
quotes.incident_not_attack: CDFW encourages the use of the term “incident” to refer to these interactions, instead of “attack,” as scientists generally agree that most white shark incidents with humans are not predatory attempts, but rather the result of exploratory bites from sharks investigating unusual objects in their environment, such as kayaks. Scientists also believe sharks may mistake people for their usual prey - seals or sea lions. The word attack assigns intent to the shark’s action that is not necessarily accurate.
quotes.rarity: Incidents where sharks bite humans are extremely rare in California.
quotes.history: Since 1950, there have been less than 250 shark incidents in California involving many species of sharks, the vast majority of which involved white sharks. Of those, fewer than 20 were fatal and all of the fatalities likely involved white sharks (see details below).
quotes.nursery: Scientists consider Southern California a nursery ground for white sharks. Pregnant sharks likely give birth in the relatively calm, warmer waters offshore and the juvenile sharks spend significant time in shallow water.
